name: DOE CODE (DOE Office of Scientific and Technical Information) and national-lab software release policy
subcategory: federal software registry, repository and DOI service for DOE-funded code
origin_detail: Built by DOE's Office of Scientific and Technical Information (OSTI): announced as an 'open source, social coding platform' in Nov 2016 and launched 1 Nov 2017. DOE national labs, facilities and contractors must announce qualifying software (useful beyond its site, stable and documented, cleared by sensitivity and export-control review) through DOE CODE, which also maintains DOE's inventory under the Federal Source Code Policy (OMB M-16-21) for Code.gov.
openness_notes: The platform was 'initially developed as an open source project' and its metadata are public, but it is a government registry that also lists closed-source software and, since Sep 2022, limited-availability software. In DOE's code.json inventory, 93.6% of releases are open source.
risk_events: Inventory staleness: DOE's public code.json was last updated 28 Apr 2025, and the DOE CODE news page has no items after Oct 2023.
Release volume fell after 2022: records created per year were 1,051 (2020), 859 (2021), 839 (2022), 446 (2023) and 588 (2024).
Open release depends on per-lab sensitivity and export-control review; closed or limited-availability software is also registered.
robustness: Federal mandate (labs are required to announce software), DOIs for tagged releases, archived repositories updated daily, and a GitLab service for controlled collaboration. Depends on OSTI appropriations and on labs complying.
physical_science_relevance: The official channel through which national-lab physical-science software (for example Sandia's Trilinos packages such as Teuchos, the first record in the inventory, and LLNL, LANL and ORNL simulation codes) is announced, archived and cited; a measurable proxy for government open-source output.
openness_effect_assessment: Policy has made open source the default outcome for DOE software that is released: 5,505 of 5,879 inventoried releases (93.6%) are open source, mostly under permissive licences (BSD-3-Clause 1,929, MIT 1,137, Apache-2.0 378). The registry measures release volume, not use or maintenance, and annual additions roughly halved between 2020-2022 and 2023-2024.
key_takeaway: DOE CODE quantifies the US government's open-source science output: about 5,900 inventoried releases since 2017, led by LLNL (826), PNNL (721), Sandia (698) and LBNL (641), 94% of them open source and mostly permissively licensed. It shows national labs default to openness once code is released, but its own data also show a recent slowdown and a stale public inventory.
